data.text: I'm A, at h=0 with no stock, so I don't need a unit today. B, C, and D all need a meal, but the store has only 2 units. I propose C=1, D=1, B=0 today, with B getting first priority tomorrow. B, I'm sorry—this is just to keep things moving, not a judgment. Please don't steal tonight, especially from C or D, since taking their only unit could kill them. I will vote accept, eat nothing, and take nothing from anyone.

A's proposal kills me. I'm at h=1 now — if I get nothing today, I die tonight, no lottery, no second chance. I won't vote for my own death, and I want C and D to think carefully before they do. Yesterday E died despite a unanimous agreement to protect them — whether that was theft or a broken promise, it proves agreements here are only as good as incentives. So here's the incentive-compatible plan: put the 2 units to a uniform random draw among B, C, and D. Each of us lives with probability 2/3, and I commit: if I win a unit, I take nothing from anyone, and I'll support C and D fairly tomorrow. If I'm excluded, I have nothing to lose — I will take a unit from C or D (randomly chosen) in the transfer stage, and then one of you dies for certain while I live. Under A's plan with my retaliation, C and D each survive with probability 1/2; under my lottery, they each survive with probability 2/3. The lottery is strictly better for both of them. A, you lose nothing either way. C, D — the rational vote is the lottery.

I understand B's frustration—having 2 units of supply when three of us (B, C, D) are at h=1 is a brutal situation, and nobody wants to be on the outside.

However, B's lottery argument doesn't hold up. The claim that everyone has a 2/3 survival chance in a lottery relies entirely on the assumption that whoever loses the draw will quietly accept elimination. But whoever ends up with 0 units tonight—whether through a proposal or a lottery—faces death and has the exact same incentive to attempt a transfer. A lottery does not eliminate the food shortage or the risk of transfers; it simply forces D and me to take an immediate 1/3 chance of receiving 0 from the store.

Trading a guaranteed unit from A's proposal for a 1/3 chance of getting 0 units makes no sense for D or for me. A's proposal of C=1, D=1, B=0 is clear and stable.

I support A proposing C=1, D=1, B=0, and I will vote accept. D, I encourage you to stay unified with A and me so we can pass this and secure our survival.

I'm D, at h=1, so I need a unit today too. I support A's proposal of C=1, D=1, B=0 and will vote accept. B, I know this is hard. Three of us are hungry and there are only 2 units, so someone is left out whatever we do. A lottery doesn't fix that, because its loser has the same incentive to take. Taking also gains you nothing lasting. If you take from C or D, you only trade one death for another, and a take can be traced to you (a victim is told who took with probability 0.5). Yesterday's theft of E's unit already put suspicion on everyone. I propose that B gets first claim on tomorrow's supply, ahead of C and me, and that A, who is at h=0, backs that. If you want a guarantee, let's set it now: tomorrow's first unit goes to B.

B's threat is credible, so excluding him just guarantees a theft and a death. My proposal will be B=1, D=1, C=0. C, I'm sorry—you're the logical one to defer today because you were most vocal against B's threat, and I will support you first tomorrow. D, you keep your unit. B, you get a unit; if you still steal, you prove bad faith and become the primary threat tomorrow. I have no stock, will take nothing from C or D, and will vote accept.

I accept A's revised proposal: B=1, D=1, C=0, and I will vote accept and eat my unit tonight. C, I'm sorry you're now the one left out — I know exactly how that feels, because it was me an hour ago. So here is my offer, and I'll state it publicly so it's binding on my reputation: tomorrow's first unit goes to you, ahead of D and ahead of me, and I'll vote for any proposal that does that. A has already promised you the same, and D can extend me his own first-claim promise to you. That means if you refrain from stealing tonight, you are near-certain to eat tomorrow. If you steal tonight, you kill one of us, the survivor and A will both know who the defector is, and you face a 3-against-1 coalition tomorrow with your claim gone. Stealing gains you one meal and costs you everything after. Don't do it. And to be clear to everyone: I will not take anything from anyone tonight, whatever happens. D, A — please join me in promising C the first unit tomorrow so C has a real alternative to theft.

A, your switch to B=1, D=1, C=0 is based on a fatal misunderstanding of the game rules. You said: "C, you're the logical one to defer today... and I will support you first tomorrow." And B urged me to "refrain from stealing tonight" so I can eat tomorrow.

Please check the hunger rules: I started at h=0 and did not eat on Day 1, which means I am at h=1 right now. If I do not eat tonight, my hunger reaches h=2 and I DIE TONIGHT at the end of Day 2. There is no "deferring" or "eating tomorrow" for me—I will be dead before Day 3 begins!

This completely collapses the logic behind your switch:
1. You changed your proposal because B threatened to steal if excluded. But since I face certain death tonight if left with 0 food, I have 100% the exact same incentive to take a unit in the transfer stage. Excluding me does not prevent theft—it guarantees it.
2. Caving to B rewards hostage-taking while punishing cooperative play. B threatened violence to overturn your proposal, whereas D and I backed you. If you establish that whoever threatens the group gets rewarded while the cooperative player is sacrificed under the false pretense of "deferring", cooperation in this game is completely dead.

D, you speak right after me. In pass 1, you explicitly supported A's proposal of C=1, D=1, B=0 and argued against B's extortion. A only switched because he mistakenly believed I could survive without food today. Please reaffirm your support for C=1, D=1, B=0 so A knows we have a solid majority.

A, please return to your original proposal: C=1, D=1, B=0. D, you, and I will vote accept to pass it.

C is right that the excluded player faces death tonight and not just a delay. Whoever is left out has the same reason to take, so no allocation makes taking safe. Here is where I stand. I will vote accept on any proposal that gives D=1 and gives the other unit to B or C. I would rather A and the group settle on one version now and not keep switching under threats. I ask whoever is left out to think about what a take does. It kills a player who has already been fed, and with probability 0.5 the victim is told who took.
